rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening time phrase may modify the preceding humiliating punishment, or serve as the object of an implied verb meaning remember or mention.
rows.anchor: The beginning of this verse is either a clause modifying humiliating punishment or the object of an implied verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the implied-verb reading, the verse calls people to remember the gathering of every human on an open, barren plain for judgment.
rows.anchor: make mention of the Day when God will

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God records people's deeds in a registry presented at Judgment; disbelievers then find every deed recorded, though they had forgotten.
rows.anchor: God keeps account of people’s deeds in a book or registry that is then presented to them on the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that God witnesses all things is linked to several verses; elsewhere the Quran says He witnesses what people do.
rows.anchor: For God is Witness over all things, see also

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The land is Madinah; those settled there in belief are its Muslims who accepted Islam before the Prophet and the Emigrants arrived.
rows.anchor: In the land refers to Madinah, and those who were settled . . . in belief before them refers to the Muslims of Madinah

rows.speaker: IK, W
rows.claim: A report says an Ansari host and his wife fed a poor man from the People of the Veranda by giving him the children's food; the Prophet praised the couple, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: The Prophet said, “Truly the dwellers of the heavens are amazed at what you two have done.” This verse was then revealed (IK, W).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Preferring others is connected to verses praising the giving of wealth despite loving it.
rows.anchor: They prefer others over themselves is related to those verses that praise giving wealth despite loving it

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Aj reads the absence of need more broadly as removing worldly attachment from the heart, so one is not attached to what passes one by.
rows.anchor: removing this world from one’s heart, so that the heart is no longer attached to what passes it by (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says that renouncing the world wins God's love, while renouncing what belongs to others wins people's love.
rows.anchor: a ḥadīth states, “Abstain from the world, and God will love you; abstain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those protected from avarice feel no need for what is destined for others.
rows.anchor: thus describes those who feel no need for what is destined for others and are thereby protected

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith calls the soul between one's sides one's worst enemy.
rows.anchor: anotherḥadīth, “Your worst enemy is the soul between your two sides.”

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet warns against oppression, a darkness on Judgment Day, and avarice, which destroyed earlier peoples and led them to shed blood and legalize the unlawful.
rows.anchor: the Prophet warned his followers, “Be on your guard against committing oppression, for oppression is a darkness on the Day of Resurrection.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some call the sūrah Makkan, its reference to the Jews in verse 6 points to a Madinan origin.
rows.anchor: internal indicators, such as the reference to the Jews in v. 6, affirm that it is from the Madinan period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name al-Jumuʿah comes from its call to gather for Friday congregational prayer.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the exhortation to gather for the Friday congregational prayer in v. 9

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is the fourth al-Musabbiḥāt, a group of sūrahs that begin by glorifying God; the others are 57, 59, 61, and 64.
rows.anchor: the fourth in the group of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah connects to the preceding one because both compare worldly commerce with the affairs of the next world.
rows.anchor: both compare the commerce of this world with the affairs of the next

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Āl likens the call to congregational prayer to the preceding sūrah's praise of believers who fight in ranks, since worshippers also stand in ranks.
rows.anchor: in ranks during prayer (Āl)

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: Āl reports that the Prophet often recited al-Jumuʿah together with the following sūrah, al-Munāfiqūn, at Friday congregational prayer.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is reported to have often recited this sūrah and the following sūrah, al-Munāfiqūn, together

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A hadith calls Friday the best day over which the sun rises, the day Adam was created, entered and removed from the Garden, and the day the Hour will come.
rows.anchor: the Hour will not come save on the day of the congregational prayer” (Q)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One report explains the name al-Jumuʿah by saying Adam's physical nature was gathered together on that day.
rows.anchor: was gathered together” (R) or

rows.speaker: Q, IK, Sy
rows.claim: Another report explains the name as the day God gathered Adam's physical nature together.
rows.anchor: Q; also see IK, Sy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah first extols the Prophet as a blessing, then warns of the Jews' failure to uphold the Torah, and finally calls Muslims to pause commerce for Friday prayer.
rows.anchor: al-Jumuʿah warns of the afflictions that befell the Jews for having failed to uphold the Torah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ummī means someone unable to read or write.
rows.anchor: indicates those who can neither read nor write

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ takes the unlettered in this context to mean the idolatrous Arabs, who had no scripture.
rows.anchor: in this context can refer to the idolatrous Arabs, who had no scripture (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R offers the broader referent of anyone without a Divine book.
rows.anchor: or to anyone without a Divine book (R; cf. 3:20)

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭs
rows.claim: JJ and Ṭs understand the Prophet's purification of the people as purification from idolatry.
rows.anchor: Purifying them refers to purification from idolatry (JJ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's teaching of Book and Wisdom is linked to the primordial covenant with all prophets, who were to believe in and help a confirming messenger.
rows.anchor: the teaching of which is part of the primordial covenant made with all prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses also describe the Prophet teaching the Book and Wisdom.
rows.anchor: This is one of several verses in which the Prophet is said to teach the Book and Wisdom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The teaching of Book and Wisdom is also associated with Abraham, Jesus, and Muhammad.
rows.anchor: The teaching of the Book and Wisdom is also mentioned in relation to Abraham (4:54), Jesus (5:110), and Muhammad (4:113)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret Wisdom here as a reference to the Prophet's sunna.
rows.anchor: some interpret Wisdom as a reference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wisdom may also mean all divinely inspired knowledge concerning this world and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: all Divinely inspired knowledge pertaining to this world and the Hereafter (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tuʿraḍūn can mean either that people are exposed or brought forth, as in the verse about being brought before their Lord.
rows.anchor: You shall be exposed translates tuʿraḍūn, which could also be rendered

rows.speaker: IK, Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: A hadith describes three arraignments on Resurrection Day: people argue and make excuses at the first two; at the third, scrolls are handed out, with some receiving them in the right hand and others in the left.
rows.anchor: some will take with their right hand and others will take with their left” (IK, Q, R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may mean nothing is hidden from God, as another verse says of the Day people come forth.
rows.anchor: nothing is hidden from God, as in 40:16, the Day when they come forth with naught concerning them hidden from God

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R says the inner states and thoughts of people will be exposed, making believers rejoice and disbelievers grieve.
rows.anchor: the inner states and thoughts of human beings will now be known, and the result will be that the believers will rejoice and the disbelievers will grieve (R)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q offers the translation “None among you shall be hidden,” meaning that no person can escape God's Judgment.
rows.anchor: None among you shall be hidden” (Q), meaning that no human being can evade God’s Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah Nūḥ most likely dates to the middle Makkan period.
rows.anchor: is most likely from the middle Makkan period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is one of four sūrahs named after Old Testament prophets; the others are Jonah, Joseph, and Abraham.
rows.anchor: named after an Old Testament prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although named for Noah, the sūrah does not tell his whole story; other aspects occur across several Quranic accounts.
rows.anchor: Although it takes the name of Noah, this sūrah does not tell his entire story.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quranic prophetic stories are guidance, not a complete historical record; the cited verse says they strengthen the Prophet's heart and bring truth, exhortation, and reminder.
rows.anchor: the function of Quranic accounts of the prophets and sacred history is not to provide a historical record

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the Bible's details about Noah's Ark construction and post-flood life, the Quran centers on his role as a warner and his people's rejection.
rows.anchor: Although the Biblical account provides details about the construction of the Ark (Genesis 6:12–16) and Noah’s life after the flood (Genesis 9)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flood is mentioned briefly, indicating that punishment is not the Quranic account's focus; like accounts of Abraham and Jesus, it emphasizes God's Mercy and Guidance.
rows.anchor: it receives no more than one line in any of them. This indicates that God’s Punishment is not the focus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives Noah's rejecting people respite until they fully reject his repeated calls; the story urges Muhammad's opponents to accept guidance or perish and reassures Muhammad that earlier messengers faced still greater defiance.
rows.anchor: God continues to grant them respite and does not send the flood until they have completely rejected his calls

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah, with Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, is one of the resolute messengers, offered as an example to Muhammad; Muslims count Muhammad among them.
rows.anchor: Noah is considered one of the resolute among the messengers (46:35)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say Noah was the first messenger, with those before him considered prophets rather than messengers.
rows.anchor: According to some, Noah was the first messenger sent by God

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q says Noah, like Muhammad, was sent to the whole world rather than to a particular people.
rows.anchor: he was sent, like Muhammad, to the entire world, rather than to a specific people (Q)
